\chapter{Finish, Prepare and Plan the Weekend}
\label{ch:terminar-preparar-fin-semana-reservar-incluir}
\hlchaptermodality{409}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can understand five common words used to finish, prepare and book a simple plan.}

Retrieve five planning words across work, food, weekend and hotel messages.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[terminar]{terminar — reach the boundary}

\label{lesson:ES-C409-terminar}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{el trabajo}, the work. Now add the action that brings it to its endpoint: \textbf{terminar}, “to finish” or “to end.”
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{termināre} meant to set a boundary or bring something to an end. Its base was \textbf{terminus}, a boundary. English \textbf{term}, \textbf{terminal} and \textbf{terminate} keep the same boundary picture. Spanish \textbf{terminar} is the everyday verb: \textbf{terminar el trabajo}, finish the work.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the regular -ar frame}]
For “I finish,” remove \textbf{-ar} and add \textbf{-o}: \textbf{termino}. After another verb, keep the infinitive: \textbf{quiero terminar}. Hear the difference between a plan and a completed statement: \textbf{quiero terminar / termino}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{terminar}
  \item \emph{terminar el trabajo}
  \item \emph{quiero terminar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To finish? (\emph{Terminar}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/terminar}{DLE: terminar}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[preparar]{preparar — make ready beforehand}

\label{lesson:ES-C409-preparar}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{el postre}, dessert. Before it is served, someone has to make it ready: \textbf{preparar un postre}, “to prepare a dessert.” You can \textbf{terminar} a task; first you may need to \textbf{preparar} its parts.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{praeparāre} joined \textbf{prae}, “before,” to \textbf{parāre}, “make ready.” Spanish \textbf{preparar} and English \textbf{prepare} preserve that family almost unchanged. The older verb \textbf{parar} is visible inside, but do not translate the modern compound as “pre-stop”: use the whole word, “prepare.”
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: prepare a thing or prepare to act}]
Use a noun directly: \textbf{preparar un postre}. Before another action, Spanish can use \textbf{prepararse para}; this lesson keeps the simpler A1 object frame.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{preparar}
  \item \emph{preparar un postre}
  \item \emph{me gusta preparar postres}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To prepare? (\emph{Preparar}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/preparar}{DLE: preparar}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el fin de semana]{el fin de semana — the week's end}

\label{lesson:ES-C409-fin-de-semana}



\begin{quote}
Spanish builds “weekend” as a transparent phrase: \textbf{el fin de semana}, literally “the end of the week.” It gives a time for a plan: \textbf{voy a preparar el postre este fin de semana}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Fin} continues Latin \textbf{fīnis}, “boundary” or “end.” \textbf{Semana} continues Late Latin \textbf{septimāna}, the seven-day period. The little \textbf{de} joins them: \textbf{fin de semana}. Learn the three words as one planning block.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one weekend, many weekends}]
For one, say \textbf{el fin de semana}. In the plural, only the first noun changes: \textbf{los fines de semana}. For a regular habit, \textbf{trabajo los fines de semana}; for one upcoming period, \textbf{este fin de semana}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el fin de semana}
  \item \emph{este fin de semana}
  \item \emph{los fines de semana}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The weekend? (\emph{El fin de semana}.)

Sources: \href{https://dle.rae.es/fin}{DLE: fin}; \href{https://dle.rae.es/semana}{DLE: semana}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[reservar]{reservar — set it aside}

\label{lesson:ES-C409-reservar}



\begin{quote}
You have chosen \textbf{el fin de semana}. To book a room for it, use \textbf{reservar}: \textbf{reservar una habitación}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{reservāre} meant “keep back” or “preserve.” That image still works: a hotel sets a room aside for you. English \textbf{reserve} is a close relative. Keep the history at that safe level; resemblance to \textbf{servir} is not a reason to invent a separate family story.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: book a thing for people}]
The thing follows directly: \textbf{reservar una habitación}. Add the people with \textbf{para}: \textbf{para dos personas}. Together: \textbf{quiero reservar una habitación para dos personas}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{reservar}
  \item \emph{reservar una habitación}
  \item \emph{para dos personas}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To reserve or book? (\emph{Reservar}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/reservar}{DLE: reservar}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[incluir]{incluir — close it inside the whole}

\label{lesson:ES-C409-incluir}



\begin{quote}
You can \textbf{reservar} a room. Now ask what comes inside the price: \textbf{¿Incluye el desayuno?}, “Does it include breakfast?”
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish borrowed \textbf{incluir} from Latin \textbf{inclūdere}, literally “close in”: \textbf{in}, “in,” plus \textbf{claudere}, “close.” English \textbf{include}, \textbf{exclude} and \textbf{conclude} share the same learned family. Something included is enclosed inside the whole.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the useful third-person form}]
The infinitive is \textbf{incluir}, but hotel messages often use \textbf{incluye}: \textbf{el precio incluye el desayuno}. In a question, keep the same form and lift the intonation: \textbf{¿Incluye el desayuno?}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{incluir}
  \item \emph{incluye el desayuno}
  \item \emph{el precio incluye el desayuno}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To include? (\emph{Incluir}.) Does it include breakfast? (\emph{¿Incluye el desayuno?})

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/incluir}{DLE: incluir}.
\end{tcolorbox}
